evidence.claim: The OECD said Mexico's solid macroeconomic framework safeguarded stability, but growth prospects were weak, investment had been weak since 2015, regulatory uncertainty from electricity and oil market changes hurt investor confidence, competition was weak, and corruption implementation gaps persisted.
evidence.title: OECD Economic Surveys: Mexico 2022
evidence.excerpt: The OECD said Mexico's solid macroeconomic framework safeguarded stability, but growth prospects were weak, investment had been weak since 2015, regulatory uncertainty from electricity and oil market changes hurt investor confidence, competition was weak, and corruption implementation gaps persisted.
evidence.source_locator: executive summary and policy recommendations around lines 3753-3755 and 4019-4040
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Major multilateral economic survey with explicit policy diagnosis and recommendations.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 baseline and policy diagnosis relevant to AMLO's year in office.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Mix of inherited baseline and ruler-period policy choices; the uncertainty and competition effects are not solely presidential but are tied to administration proposals and governance choices.
contrary_evidence: The OECD also said Mexico's macro framework remained solid and stability was preserved.
Some weaknesses predated AMLO, so this is not pure ruler attribution.

evidence.claim: The World Bank approved a US$700 million operation tied to policies to simplify the business environment for small firms, promote financial inclusion, strengthen sustainable economic management, and expand support for vulnerable groups, rural areas, migrants, and women.
evidence.title: The World Bank and Mexico work together to foster inclusive and sustainable economic growth
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank approved a US$700 million operation tied to policies to simplify the business environment for small firms, promote financial inclusion, strengthen sustainable economic management, and expand support for vulnerable groups, rural areas, migrants, and women.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official World Bank press release describing the policy package and the government actions it supports.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 policy support during AMLO's presidency.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Supports ruler-period policy aims and implementation conditions, but the World Bank describes government policy actions rather than personal presidential execution in each detail.
contrary_evidence: The document is supportive and does not assess adverse side effects or implementation quality.
It is a policy-operation announcement, not an outcome evaluation.

evidence.claim: The finance ministry described the 2023 budget package as balanced, realistic, and prudent; said debt would remain stable and sustainable; kept no new taxes; and proposed 3.6 percent of GDP in physical investment including infrastructure plus protected social programs.
evidence.title: Comunicado No. 64 Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público entrega Paquete Económico 2023 al Congreso
evidence.publisher: Secretaría de Hacienda y Crédito Público, Gobierno de México
evidence.excerpt: The finance ministry described the 2023 budget package as balanced, realistic, and prudent; said debt would remain stable and sustainable; kept no new taxes; and proposed 3.6 percent of GDP in physical investment including infrastructure plus protected social programs.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Direct government budget statement with explicit fiscal and spending commitments.
evidence.period_fit: Direct late-2022 ruler-period fiscal policy evidence.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly attributable to AMLO's government through the finance ministry and budget package.
contrary_evidence: The source is self-reporting and may overstate prudence or future sustainability.
It is a budget plan and forward projection, not implementation proof.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Mexico's anti-inflation subsidies cost about 575 billion pesos in 2022, with 430 billion pesos going to gasoline-price subsidies, and officials said the measures helped ease the pain of ordinary people.
evidence.title: Mexico anti-inflation subsidies come with $28 billion price tag
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Mexico's anti-inflation subsidies cost about 575 billion pesos in 2022, with 430 billion pesos going to gasoline-price subsidies, and officials said the measures helped ease the pain of ordinary people.
evidence.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Subsidies from the Mexican government...'
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters wire reporting on an official cost estimate and the policy rationale.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributable to AMLO's government; the policy was publicly defended by officials speaking alongside him.
contrary_evidence: The subsidies were expensive and could weaken fiscal space.
Reuters notes the benefit claim comes from officials, not independent measurement.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that López Obrador's plan to increase state control of power generation was defeated in parliament after opposition parties said it would hurt investment and breach international obligations.
evidence.title: Mexican president's contentious electricity overhaul defeated in Congress
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that López Obrador's plan to increase state control of power generation was defeated in parliament after opposition parties said it would hurt investment and breach international obligations.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a major legislative defeat involving an AMLO priority bill.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 evidence of a policy fight affecting investment rules.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The proposal was AMLO's, but the legislative defeat shows institutional resistance rather than successful executive capture.
contrary_evidence: The article reflects opponents' claims about investment harm, not a court finding.
The bill failed, so the most aggressive version did not become law.

evidence.claim: Reuters said Mexico risked missing an investment windfall from the semiconductor boom because firms were worried about power supply, fossil-fuel dependence, and weak incentives.
evidence.title: Energy politics cloud Mexican bid to join U.S. semiconductor rush
evidence.excerpt: Reuters said Mexico risked missing an investment windfall from the semiconductor boom because firms were worried about power supply, fossil-fuel dependence, and weak incentives.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters summary of investor concerns and policy constraints in late 2022.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 evidence about investment conditions under AMLO.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Attributed to the AMLO-era policy environment, especially energy and incentive settings, rather than a single personal decision.
contrary_evidence: The story is forward-looking and does not show realized lost investment yet.
It identifies business concerns, not a formal government policy finding.

evidence.claim: Reuters reported that Pemex was under pressure to resume debt repayments despite López Obrador's promise that the government would pay them until 2024, with about 1 billion euros due on a bond.
evidence.title: Exclusive-Mexico's Pemex under pressure to resume financial debt payments
evidence.excerpt: Reuters reported that Pemex was under pressure to resume debt repayments despite López Obrador's promise that the government would pay them until 2024, with about 1 billion euros due on a bond.
evidence.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Mexico's cash-strapped state oil firm...'
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Reuters reporting on a specific financing problem and prior presidential commitment.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 evidence of fiscal and SOE stress during the ruler-period.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Relevant to AMLO because Pemex support was a signature government policy, though the company and finance ministry execute the payments.
contrary_evidence: The source shows continuing support for a strategic firm, which can be framed as stability rather than pure mismanagement.
This is a debt-service snapshot, not a full assessment of Pemex reform.

evidence.claim: The OECD said Mexico still had not concluded its first foreign-bribery case, had made little progress on key enforcement recommendations, and still lacked specific whistleblower protection legislation more than a decade after the recommendation.
evidence.title: Mexico should urgently address long-standing concerns over foreign bribery enforcement and protect whistleblowers
evidence.excerpt: The OECD said Mexico still had not concluded its first foreign-bribery case, had made little progress on key enforcement recommendations, and still lacked specific whistleblower protection legislation more than a decade after the recommendation.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official OECD monitoring statement with clear compliance findings.
evidence.period_fit: Direct 2022 corruption-enforcement evidence during AMLO's term.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The enforcement gap spans institutions under AMLO's government, though it reflects longer-running state capacity problems as well.
contrary_evidence: This is about foreign bribery enforcement, not the whole domestic corruption picture.
The OECD notes some awareness-raising progress.

evidence.claim: Bloomberg Línea said Victoria Rodríguez Ceja, a public-finance economist with more than 20 years in public finance, was nominated by AMLO to head Banxico, but the appointment occurred amid questions about the bank's autonomy.
evidence.title: Victoria Rodríguez Ceja
evidence.excerpt: Bloomberg Línea said Victoria Rodríguez Ceja, a public-finance economist with more than 20 years in public finance, was nominated by AMLO to head Banxico, but the appointment occurred amid questions about the bank's autonomy.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Profile piece with direct attribution and a clear summary of the appointment and autonomy debate.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Directly tied to AMLO because he nominated her; the source also shows the limit that the central bank retained formal autonomy.
contrary_evidence: Concerns about autonomy cut against a clean competence narrative.
The piece is descriptive rather than a full evaluation of outcomes.

evidence.claim: BBVA Research summarized Coneval's 2022 measurement, saying 46.8 million people were in poverty and 9.1 million in extreme poverty, while access to health worsened between 2018 and 2022.
evidence.title: Mexico | Poverty decreases at its lowest level (36.3%); but, access to health deteriorates
evidence.excerpt: BBVA Research summarized Coneval's 2022 measurement, saying 46.8 million people were in poverty and 9.1 million in extreme poverty, while access to health worsened between 2018 and 2022.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Independent research summary of the official poverty measurement with explicit 2022 numbers.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective on 2022 household welfare and distribution.
evidence.ruler_attribution: Only partly attributable to AMLO; the results reflect labor-market, social-policy, and structural factors over several years.
contrary_evidence: Health access deterioration is a significant negative offset.
Extreme poverty did not improve as strongly as headline poverty.

evidence.claim: The World Bank said Mexico's official multidimensional poverty rate fell from 43.2 percent in 2016 to 36.3 percent in 2022, lifting 5.4 million people out of poverty and noting that the improvement was driven mainly by labor-market outcomes, including minimum-wage increases.
evidence.title: Mexico Overview: Development news, research, data
evidence.excerpt: The World Bank said Mexico's official multidimensional poverty rate fell from 43.2 percent in 2016 to 36.3 percent in 2022, lifting 5.4 million people out of poverty and noting that the improvement was driven mainly by labor-market outcomes, including minimum-wage increases.
evidence.source_confidence_reason: Official World Bank country overview summarizing the 2022 poverty outcome and its drivers.
evidence.period_fit: Retrospective but directly about 2022 outcomes under AMLO.
evidence.ruler_attribution: The World Bank attributes the improvement mainly to labor-market outcomes, which supports AMLO-era policy relevance, but the source does not isolate presidential causation cleanly.
contrary_evidence: The page also says Mexico has underperformed on growth and inclusion over the long run.
Later publication date makes this retrospective rather than contemporaneous.

unresolved_gaps: Direct 2022 evidence on AMLO's personal control over civilian-nuclear safety appointments, regulatory discipline, or command-side decisions is thin.
There is no Mexico-originating war, proxy conflict, or coercive peace leverage in 2022, so the dossier is mostly diplomatic posture rather than operational conflict conduct.
Specific chain-of-command evidence for some police, military, and intelligence abuses remains incomplete, especially for local versus federal responsibility.
Some of the evidence about electoral reform and media pressure is rhetorical or journalistic rather than a direct legal finding of intent to entrench power.
The causal split between AMLO policy, inherited weakness, and global shocks is still only partially recoverable for 2022 poverty, inflation, and investment outcomes.
Independent post-launch quality and outcome audits for IMSS-Bienestar, education recovery, and related welfare programs are thinner than the rollout record.
Direct documentary evidence of personal enrichment, hidden financial benefit, or knowing approval of surveillance remains limited.
Durability and post-launch independent audits for AIFA, Dos Bocas, IMSS-Bienestar, and the education programs are thinner than the implementation record.
